Question: Can you explain the difference between rigor mortis and muscle spasm?
Answer: Rigor mortis is due to the exhaustion of ATP and the the mobilization of calcium from its stores into the cytosol to constitute calcium overload after death as organelles deteriorate, glycogen stores are depleted and anaerobic respiration stops. Calcium is needed for contraction as it enables cross-bridge (cross-link) between the myosin (thick filament) head and actin (thin filament), so increased availability of calcium in the cytosol increases the intensity of this event. Calcium binds to the troposin on the actin filament and permits tropomyosin on the actin to move out of the way, allowing the myosin head, carrying ADP, to bind to actin, contract and pull actin centrally. Relaxation is afforded by the replacement of ADP on the myosin head by ATP, as this detaches the myosin head from actin and allows actins to drift peripherally away from the central line. With increased calcium and reduced ATP, the muscle therefore remains in a state of sustained contractions. Muscle spasm is due to fast motor signals being delivered into skeletal muscles, and they cause unending contractions (contractions without intervening relaxations) of muscle fibers which lead to synchronized tetany that represents repeated contractions of the muscle fibers in unison, when they are not yet fully relaxed, and means that new contractions are piggbacking upon preceding contractions. Tetany in the skeletal muscle during cramps (spasms) happens because the duration of the muscle fiber action potential is much smaller than that of muscle contraction itself, so that a new signal arrives while the preceding one is still causing contraction although long gone (left or departed the muscle fiber), and these activities are synchronized in the entire muscle. For the heart where the duration of the action potential of the cardiac muscle cell is the same as that of its contraction proper and all happening in phase, the incoming action potential meets the previous one still in play and hence the muscle fiber is still refractory. The new signal simply fizzles out. A signal can only stimulate the heart when the previous one is gone, the muscle contraction done, and the muscle is fully relaxed.

Question: Can hypertension medicines be stopped after high blood pressure is under control?
Answer: No. Blood pressure drugs are not a cure. They lower blood pressure by antagonizing the rise in blood pressure, but do not change the underlying pathology behind high blood pressure. Arteriosclerosis, plaque in the arteries, whose deposition increases with age, is associated with high blood pressure. Although its build-up can be slowed down by adopting a healthful lifestyle, once established, little can be done to clear the plaque. Plaque reduces compliance of the arteries, which compliance is a physiological mechanism used by the body to regulate blood pressure. Besides, blood pressure regulation has a timeline above which the neuronal feedback from blood to the brain to make these adjustments is lost. Tissue perfusion or blood flow is the prime goal of the pumping heart. Once compliance is lost through arteriosclerosis, the heart attempts to pump much harder to achieve its goal. However, met with obstruction, from stiff and narrowed blood vessels, less blood leaves the heart and the stroke volume falls, as the heart rate and total peripheral resistance rise. Tissue perfusion falls even much lower. Blood pressure is thus reset at a higher level in a bid to imaintain optimal cardiac output, blood flow and tissue perfusion. High blood pressure drugs pharmacologically dilate the stiff blood arteries and/or slow the heart and/or reduce blood volume to increase arterial compliance, blood flow and tissue perfusion. If you stop taking the drug(s) that had lowered your blood pressure, and with this pathology still in place, blood pressure rises back up again. And sometimes to a much higher value. That said for essential hypertenstion, high blood pressure due to a known, correctable, cause like kidney failure, can go away once the underlying kidney dysfunction has been corrected, but stopping treatment without the correction will not help. Lifestyle changes like exercise, low salt intake and weight loss may lower blood pressure by reducing the burden on blood vessels and the heart and this will reduce the need for drugs in borderline hypertension cases.
